newsitem.title: NORWAY: NATO moves closer to new Bosnia commitment.
newsitem.headline: NATO moves closer to new Bosnia commitment.

text.p: NATO countries moved closer on Wednesday towards a commitment to keep thousands of troops in Bosnia next year after the mandate of the current peace mission runs out on December 20.

NATO diplomats said the Atlantic alliance's 16 defence ministers, meeting informally in this Norwegian port city, accepted that some sort of force would probably be necessary to stop the country slipping back into war.

"Nobody said we did not need a Bosnia force...it is an option which can no longer be kept in the background," one NATO official said. "There was an overwhelming consensus that although we have achieved a lot, we have not achieved enough to say that peace has been achieved," he added.

Alliance diplomats said the ministers wanted the military to begin a study of the tasks that any force would be required to undertake and the risks it would face, but said it was premature to discuss its size or mandate.
"We must decide on force aims before we can even discuss its size," a senior alliance diplomat told Reuters.

NATO sources said that, although U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry did not explicitly say U.S. troops would be in the force, there was broad agreement that it would include the same countries as the current Implementation Force (IFOR).

The U.S. now has 15,000 troops serving in the 52,000-strong IFOR force, which was sent in last December to police the Dayton peace accords. Britain and France, the other main contributors, would not remain without a U.S. ground presence.
The issue is sensitive in the United States ahead of the November 5 presidential election there. President Bill Clinton originally said the troops would be home by the end of the year.
NATO officials said the military would be instructed at the next meeting of the alliance's policy-making North Atlantic Council to start work on four options for 1997.
These would involve:
-- total withdrawal of existing force in line with the current political instructions.
-- a deterrence force limited to preventing an outbreak of fresh fighting.
-- a deterrence force with a wider mandate to provide a general security framework in which emerging civilian structures could begin to function.
-- a force fulfilling deterrence and giving much wider support to civilian reconstruction efforts, including freedom of movement for refugees and returnees.

"There was a general consensus that the force has to have the freedom to do its job," the official said, adding that ministers all insisted on the need to have continued Russian involvement in the follow-on force.

He also said that the allies all agreed any new force must conform with the requirments of Dayton, be equipped with a U.N. mandate, have the full consent of all parties and have the means to protect itself.

The defence ministers, leaving some of the more delicate issues to be resolved by foreign ministers, said any new force could only be despatched as part of a wider political framework setting out the international community's medium-term aims.
They also stressed it must have a clear timetable for handover to civilian authorities and avoid any "open-ended commitment to maintain a force" in the Balkan country.

NATO sources said NATO's Supreme Allied Commander in Europe (SACEUR), General George Joulwan, had briefed the ministers on the need to move from an implementation to stabilisation force, but wanted "clear political instructions". "Joulwan kept stressing the need for clarity," one diplomat said.

Other diplomats said there was a general acceptance that the coming year could produce more problems than this year with the return of refugees and the emergence of legitimate institutions complicating NATO's work.

The ministers also agreed the current force would not begin a withdrawal until after municipal elections, now set for late November. Officials said the alliance was committed to providing the same sort of security blanket it gave to countrywide polls on September 14, but emphasised any postponement would not delay the start of the current withdrawal plans.
